source.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
source.authors: Tavish Mankash; Vardhaman Kalloli; Keshava Prasad; Deepan Muthirayan

page_placements.theme: Architecture, training and regularization shape specialization

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether changing output-coordinate sharing changes localization and readability, using controlled latent-cause tasks and language-model coordinate evaluations rather than the original toy-superposition method.
record.gate_note: The reported latent-cause localization, expert-output overlap, native-coordinate specificity, and SAE-feature specificity are results on representation localization or overlap. Language-model loss and throughput, router-screen results, and request detection or steering are not rows: they do not measure the claim versions' representational geometry. The geometry and request interventions are deliberately induced case studies, not evidence that the behavior arises without intervention. Cited findings from other work are not counted.
record.test_reason: This is mainly an architecture paper. MoWE forces experts to write to disjoint coordinates, and most rows report that design's own localization, not superposition arising on its own. The one result bearing on a version is V4. In a 103M dense LM, TopK SAE features trained on the FFN update score clearly higher description specificity than native coordinates or a random rotation (0.489 vs 0.375/0.390). Post-block and pilot SAEs show the same, so it is a new-setting test of V4. Nothing in the study manipulates feature importance or capacity, so it does not test V2. The MoWE zero-overlap rows hold by construction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that sparse routing gives conditional computation, while fixed disjoint output addresses localize known causes and make native FFN coordinates more specific. Standard MoE's native coordinates are no more readable than a random rotation. Native MoWE is comparable to a dense TopK SAE (CI includes zero), and SAEs still add structure. The case studies are narrow, one-next-token demonstrations.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates a read-all, write-disjoint routed FFN architecture, controlled cause-localization metrics, and automated coordinate/SAE description evaluations; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported readability differs across architecture and representation type; MoWE exceeds dense in 18 of 19 layers. The study also reports distinct results for native versus random-rotated bases and for FFN-update versus post-block SAE sites.

fits_no_version.finding: On the known-cause task, dense and standard-MoE residual coordinates mix many causes, though the 128 dims exceed the 32 causes (Fig 5, figure only). Routing to disjoint output coordinates localizes causes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cause mixing in coordinates without a privileged basis can occur without capacity pressure; output-basis constraints localize it (architecture-induced monosemanticity).

fits_no_version.finding: Disjoint-write MoE (MoWE) native FFN-output coordinates have higher judge specificity than dense (0.523 vs 0.375) and standard MoE (0.268). Standard-MoE coordinates are no more specific than a random rotation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural write-disjointness makes native output coordinates more interpretable; sparse routing alone does not.

record.problems: The all-layer interpretability comparison uses one checkpoint per architecture; the loss comparison has two runs per architecture. The main SAE audit evaluates live features only, with substantial dead-feature fractions. Coordinate specificity relies on an automated language-model judge. The paper itself notes that the controlled models are not exactly compute matched, and that its intervention demonstrations are narrow and do not establish broad feature completeness or robustness.
record.rows_left_out: No results on the tested versions were omitted due to the row cap. Language-model loss, throughput, routing-regularization screens, prediction accuracy in clustered reconstruction, and deliberately induced case-study steering were not entered as rows because they do not directly measure the tested versions' representational localization or SAE-feature specificity.

untested.parts: Not tested: no overcomplete sparse features, near-orthogonal geometry, sparsity transition, or geometric arrangement.
Not tested: there is no manipulation of feature importance or capacity. Zero overlap in MoWE is imposed by design, and the toy task has more dimensions (128) than causes (32).
Not tested: whether features are spread across many neurons (only non-privileged FFN-output coordinates are examined), and whether SAEs recover all relevant features.
Not tested: completeness, stability or canonicality of SAE features. The paper only cites that dictionaries need not be unique.

missing.what: SAE reconstruction quality: validation FVU 0.0622 (dense) and 0.00277 (MoWE), with exactly 38 active features. Needed to judge how well the dictionary recovers activations.
Pilot raw purities: dense SAE 0.4193 vs native 0.2973 vs rotation 0.2644; normalized gain 0.2107 vs 0.0447.
The dense SAE beats its rotation in a stated number of layers? Only MoWE-vs-dense SAE layer wins (15/19) are given. Across-layer SD for the dense SAE is 0.065.

record.verdict_notes: The record treated an architecture comparison as a V2 test. Nothing manipulates feature importance or capacity, and MoWE's zero overlap is built in, so all V2 links are removed. Dense FFN-output coordinates lack a privileged basis: native and rotation both score 0.375. These are not neurons, so they say little about neuron-level superposition. All interpretability scores come from one LLM judge (GPT-5.6 Luna) and one checkpoint per architecture, and only live SAE features were scored (dead fractions 0.524 dense, 0.701 MoWE).

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test overcomplete sparse features, nearly orthogonal overlapping directions, a sparsity-dependent superposition transition, or regular geometric arrangements.

It compares shared and disjoint expert output coordinates and measures localization/readability, but does not test whether importance determines which features get dedicated dimensions or establish the full capacity-allocation mechanism.
It does not test whether polysemanticity arises from alternative causes independent of capacity pressure.

The SAE evaluation measures automated description specificity for live features, not whether features are distributed across many neurons or whether the dictionary recovers all relevant model features.
The paper says an SAE dictionary need not be unique or complete, but does not test canonicality, completeness, or stability in its own experiments.
It evaluates scalar coordinates and multi-coordinate slices, but does not test whether the underlying superposed features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.
